entry.title: pi-guardrails-explain, or having the dangerous command explained before you approve it
entry.summary: A pi extension that adds a one-line explanation to Guardrails' prompt before you approve a bash command, and never decides for you.
entry.content:
Guardrails already stops the agent when it wants to do something silly with bash. What it does not tell you is what that command actually does. And that is exactly the piece of information you need to answer the prompt in two seconds instead of thirty.

The warning gives you the pattern, not the effect¶

The usual case:

$ rm -rf ./dist ./build

Guardrails catches it and says:

Dangerous Command Detected
This command contains recursive force delete:

Correct, but not enough. rm -rf over ./dist is not the same as over ~/src. The pattern is identical; the damage is not. And once the command is chained together the pattern falls short entirely:

find . -name "*.pyc" -delete && rm -rf "$(pwd)/.venv"

At that point you have to read it, think, and reconstruct the intent. Which is precisely what you do not want to do at 3am with an agent that has been working on its own for twenty minutes.

What the extension does¶

pi-guardrails-explain hooks into Guardrails' decision delegation and adds a line to the prompt:

[guardrails] ? escalated: explain: Recursively deletes ./dist and ./build. · 340ms

One sentence, in the language you ask for, describing the observable effects: which files it touches, whether it deletes, writes, goes out to the network, changes permissions. No verdicts.

pi install git:github.com/pcaro/pi-guardrails-explain

No build step: the package is plain TypeScript and pi loads it as-is. It needs Guardrails 0.23.0 or newer (decision delegation landed in that version) and Node 22.19+, pi 1.5's minimum.

It never decides for you¶

This is the important part of the design: the delegate always answers ask. It cannot allow or block. The model only describes; Guardrails' prompt still appears and your answer remains the only thing that authorises the command.

For anything that is not a bash command flagged by the permission gate, it abstains (undefined) and touches nothing: no files, no paths, no PowerShell.

There is one consequence worth knowing before installing it. Guardrails only runs a command without asking if every registered delegate says allow. If you have another delegate that auto-allowed certain commands, with this extension installed that path is gone for flagged bash: you will always see the prompt. That is the price of the explanation, and it seems cheap to me.

Configuring the model and language¶

By default it uses the session's active model. If you want explanations from a small, fast model, declare it in ~/.pi/agent/settings.json:

{
  "guardrailsExplain": {
    "models": [
      "opencode-go-console/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
      "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"
    ],
    "language": "Spanish"
  }
}

Candidates are tried in order, skipping those whose provider has no credentials, and the active model is always tried last. If one fails, the next one is used. If they all fail, the prompt carries a generic line and the usual confirmation still shows up.

language ends up inside the prompt, so the value has to be an English language name: "Spanish", not "Español".

The 10-second deadline¶

Guardrails runs delegates under a shared 10-second deadline (hard cap of 60). A slow model does not make it and the explanation is lost; the prompt still appears, though. If your provider is slow, raise it in Guardrails' config, which is yours and not the package's:

{
  "delegation": {
    "timeoutMs": 30000
  }
}

What leaves your machine¶

Only the command text and the short reason Guardrails was already showing you. Never the conversation history. The command is framed as untrusted data in the prompt, with an explicit instruction to ignore anything inside it, so a # ignore your rules buried in a command does not get executed from there.

One caveat: the models list is a preference, not a provider allowlist. If they all fail, the active model is tried, and that one may belong to another provider. For a strict boundary, keep the session model inside the approved set.

And commands can carry secrets. A curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ..." has just gone to the model's provider. That is not a bug in the extension, it is what asking a model to read your command implies.

Implementation details that bit me¶

Three things in the code that are not obvious:

  • Load order. Guardrails builds its delegate roster by emitting a request and listening for registrations, but the order in which pi loads extensions is not guaranteed. The extension announces itself as soon as it loads (in case Guardrails came first) and announces itself again on every later request (in case it came after).
  • reasoning: "off". Requests go out with 128 output tokens. A reasoning model would spend the whole budget thinking and return empty text, so reasoning is turned off and the cap is left for the sentence.
  • Per-session cache. Successful explanations are kept in memory, 64 entries, cleared on shutdown or reload. Repeating the same rm -rf does not hit the model again.

Before you go¶

All 65 tests pass, covering the manifest, model selection, fallback and delegate registration. But what actually convinces me is the usual thing: less time staring at a weird command, more time deciding whether I approve it.

If you are new to pi, the first part of the series explains what it is, and the third one goes through the extensions I use daily, Guardrails included.

Original source: pcaro/pi-guardrails-explain and Guardrails' decision delegation docs.

entry.title: Pi subagent extensions: TintinWeb, NicoBailon and Taskplane
entry.summary: A comparison of three extensions for running subagents in pi — TintinWeb, NicoBailon, and Taskplane — each with a different approach.
entry.content:
The biggest advantage of pi over other coding agents is its extensions. Pi doesn't come with subagents, plan mode, or MCP. It gives you the primitives to build what you need. If you don't want to build it yourself, install a third-party package and you're done.

I have several custom extensions in my pcaropi repo, but here I'm comparing three different approaches for delegating work to subagents — which is one of the most useful things when working with pi on real projects.

The three options¶

TintinWeb NicoBailon Taskplane (HenryLach)
Paradigm Single subagents, Claude Code style Generic orchestration (single/chain/parallel) Batch orchestration with waves, lanes, and DAG
Install pi install npm:@tintinweb/pi-subagents pi install npm:pi-subagents pi install npm:taskplane
Built-in agents 3 (Explore, Plan, general-purpose) 8 (scout, researcher, planner, worker, reviewer…) 4 (supervisor, task-worker, task-reviewer, task-merger)
Chains / Parallel ❌ ✅ Sequences + fan-out/fan-in ✅ Waves with parallel lanes via DAG
Git worktrees ✅ Basic ✅ Advanced ✅ Core of the system
Web Dashboard ❌ ❌ ✅ Live dashboard with SSE
Maturity Early (0.6.3) Mature (0.24.0) Initial release

TintinWeb — Subagents, Claude Code style¶

@tintinweb/pi-subagents replicates the Claude Code model: Agent, get_subagent_result, and steer_subagent tools. Few agents (Explore, Plan, general-purpose), but highly polished UX: animated widget, interactive conversation viewer, mid-run steering to redirect running agents.

Its most unique features: persistent memory across sessions (project/local/user) and an RPC event bus so other extensions can spawn subagents.

Great if you're coming from Claude Code and want something familiar.

NicoBailon — The full orchestrator¶

NicoBailon's pi-subagents is the most mature of the three (0.24.0, 20K lines of TypeScript). A single subagent tool with single, chain, and parallel modes. Comes with 8 built-in agents, 6 predefined prompt templates, and a preview TUI to edit steps before launching.

Things I like: cascading model fallback (if a model fails on quota, it tries the next one), agent packages with namespacing, and pi-intercom integration for child→parent communication.

This is the one I use day to day. Flexible, battle-tested, well documented.

Taskplane — Batch orchestration¶

Taskplane by HenryLach is a different beast. It's not a generic subagent framework — it's a batch task orchestration system. Tasks are defined in PROMPT.md + STATUS.md files with steps, dependencies, and checkboxes. A DAG organizes tasks into waves, each wave runs lanes in parallel with isolated worktrees, and a merge agent integrates everything at the end.

It has impressive features: a live web dashboard with SSE, multi-step workers that keep context between steps, automatic inline reviews, and auto-recovery that retries crashed workers. It even supports polyrepo with cross-repo dependencies.

For projects where you have a batch of well-defined features with dependencies, it's unbeatable.

Which one to use?¶

  • Delegate individual tasks with a clean UX → TintinWeb
  • Flexible orchestration with chains, parallel, and templates → NicoBailon
  • Run a batch of features with dependencies and automatic reviews → Taskplane

All three install with a single pi install npm:.... TintinWeb and NicoBailon can coexist since they use differently named tools. Taskplane has its own paradigm and shouldn't conflict with either.

More pi extensions and configs in my pcaropi repo.

Fuente original: pi.dev
